analysis.one_liner: Ends the consumer bureau's independent funding and makes it compete for money each year.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 29 House Republicans, never got a hearing or vote and died in the House Financial Services Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is the one major financial regulator whose budget does not depend on Congress: it draws its money directly from the Federal Reserve's earnings. This bill would cut that off and make the bureau get its funding through the normal yearly congressional spending process. Supporters frame that as budget accountability; the practical effect is that Congress — where the banking and lending industries are heavily represented — could squeeze the bureau's budget every year, weakening the agency that polices banks, debt collectors, and payday lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday lenders, and debt collectors that the bureau fines and sues would face an agency that has to come back to Congress for money every year, giving their allies in Congress an annual point of leverage to trim its enforcement budget. Members of Congress who want more control over the bureau would gain that lever.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act that let the bureau draw its funding from Federal Reserve earnings outside the annual appropriations process [S2][S3].
Authorizes appropriations for fiscal years 2021 and 2022 "such sums as may be necessary" through the regular spending process instead [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers would bear the cost: the bureau that returns money to cheated customers and polices predatory lending, junk fees, and abusive debt collection would have its budget exposed to an annual congressional vote, which history shows is the easiest way to hobble a regulator without ever voting down a single enforcement action.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers who rely on the bureau

drawbacks.text: The good-faith objection is real: the bureau is the only major financial regulator not subject to the appropriations process, so its roughly half-billion-dollar budget passes with no congressional line-item review and limited spending accountability [S2][S3].

The acknowledged cost: funding through annual appropriations makes the bureau's work hostage to budget standoffs and to whichever party controls one chamber, rather than to any finding that a particular enforcement action was wrong.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is legitimate on its face, but it rests on the assumption that Congress would use its new leverage responsibly. The more likely real-world effect is structural: an agency that wins against payday lenders and debt collectors would have to survive a yearly budget vote in the very institution those industries lobby. The bill offers procedural tidiness at the price of the enforcement teeth ordinary consumers rely on.

outcome.mechanism: A Republican congressman introduced it in February 2021 and it was sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which was run by Democrats and never scheduled it for anything; it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, joined by 21 original Republican cosponsors from the Financial Services Committee [S3].

Under current law, the CFPB is funded by transfers from Federal Reserve earnings, outside the annual appropriations process; the bill would eliminate that and bring it into the regular appropriations process [S2].

It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on February 4, 2021, and the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
All 28 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bureau's independent funding survived the Congress untouched, so consumers kept an agency that cannot be starved by a single chamber's budget writer; the banks and lenders seeking appropriations control did not get it.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic chair who controlled the committee's calendar never let the bill advance.

industries.note: The bill would make the bureau that polices overdraft fees, junk fees, and unfair practices depend on a yearly congressional appropriation, giving industry allies a recurring chance to trim its budget. Consumers would bear the cost in weaker enforcement and smaller refunds.
The bureau is among the chief regulators of high-cost small-dollar lending; an appropriations-funded bureau is easier to defund, so a weaker watchdog is worth a great deal to these lenders.
Debt collection is a core CFPB enforcement target; the bill's funding change would raise the odds the bureau's enforcement capacity gets squeezed in a budget fight.
